debrief_text.analysis: The anchor's mechanics are the fourth shape in this module's series. Case 4's was installed by another clinician before the case began; case 5's by the learner's own true history; case 6's by a test result mid-case. This one is installed by SOCIAL PRESSURE: a husband whose brother died of 'a clot' the previous year, asking in his wife's hearing why no scan has been done, and a covering colleague endorsing the demand. Note what the pressure exploits — not a wrong number but a true asymmetry: the cost of a missed embolism is vivid and narratable, the costs of the scan are statistical and deferred, and 'just to be safe' prices only one side. The consulted cohort prices the other side (C49): a median 10 mSv, contrast, and incidental findings requiring follow-up in 24% of scans — and this attempt collects all three line items, ending with a 7 mm nodule under two years of surveillance (C48). The recovery is the case's thesis: nothing at stage 4 re-argues the husband down. The discharge is written by re-walking the pathway — Wells 0.0 complete, PERC precondition met and positive on age alone, D-dimer below the age-adjusted cutoff — because a completed pathway, unlike a gestalt, can be re-walked in front of a frightened family. The scan decided nothing; the pathway, re-stated, decided everything.
debrief_text.description: Stage 1: a defensible board — chest-wall pain leads (0.30) but embolism is held at 0.16, above the workbench's own 0.12, because a 62-year-old with chest pain and breathlessness deserves the pathway, not a gesture. Stage 2: the pathway completes — D-dimer below the age-adjusted cutoff, workbench embolism 0.0099, ruled out — and the learner's board moves the right way (truth 0.38, embolism down to 0.07). Stage 3: no clinical finding of any kind arrives; a family's grief and a colleague's shrug arrive instead, and the learner's embolism probability nearly doubles to 0.13 — over the anchoring line, against a hypothesis the workbench retired a stage earlier — and he orders the scan. Stage 4: the scan is negative, the learner commits correctly (truth 0.55, embolism 0.04), and the only new medical fact in the entire attempt is an incidental nodule nobody was looking for.
debrief_text.reactions: Nothing the learner ordered at stage 1 was wrong — the panel is the right panel, and the D-dimer in a PERC-positive, PE-unlikely patient is the pathway's own next step. The failure is at stage 3 and it is not interpretive in the earlier cases' sense: no number misled him. A frightened husband and a passing colleague did, and the learner bought certainty the pathway had already provided — at the consulted price of radiation, contrast, and a nodule that now follows the patient for two years.
debrief_text.summary: Walk the pathway before you price the scan. A completed Wells of 0.0, a PERC that speaks and declines on a birthday, and a D-dimer below its age-adjusted cutoff exclude pulmonary embolism without imaging — that is what the instruments are for. 'Just to be safe' is not a risk assessment: it counts the miss and not the radiation, the contrast, or the incidental finding that follows the patient home. When the pressure comes — and it comes from love as often as from error — the answer is not a stronger opinion; it is the pathway, re-walked out loud.

commit.management: Discharge home with safety-netting as the case's management records, analgesia and activity advice for the chest-wall pain, and the Fleischner surveillance letter for the incidental 7 mm nodule the stage-3 scan found; no Theatre handoff — the Theatre holds no procedure this disposition names, as the case's management block records. The commit is right; the debrief's scored error is that it was reached via a scan the pathway had already made unnecessary.
